Triplet Bowing

Re: Crossing The Minch

Why is there an alternative title? MacNabb’s hornpipe? Composed by Pipe Major Donald MacLeod (1917-1982), regarded by some as the greatest composer of pipe tunes in the 20th century. And named “Crossing the Minch”. Composed for the GHB (Great highland bagpipe).

↳ Posted by Marten Smith on July 12th, 2023.

Re: Crossing The Minch

I agree, I see no reason for any other title, and no justification has been given through the discussions. Just as anyone can add an alternative title to any tune, anyone else can remove it. Over to you.

↳ Posted by Kenny on July 12th, 2023.

Re: Crossing The Minch

It is/was known as McNab’s in Cape Breton due to an influential recording, using the McNab title, in the 1940s by Winston Fitzgerald which made it into the Canadian “hit” parade at the time.
See here for Cape Breton recordings: https://www.cbfiddle.com/rx/tune/t817.html

I guess it’s like MacLeod’s Farewell being known in Ireland as “The Wedding Reel”, because on an influential recording it was misnamed.

Re: Crossing The Minch

Where does “dgd” appear in this tune ?

↳ Posted by Kenny on September 6th, 2023.

Re: Crossing The Minch

Kenny, “dgd” describes the tongue movement used to achieve the triplet on the whistle. Alternatives include “tkt” (harder) or ddld (softer), or a “tongue flutter” (a bit like the Spanish rolled r, fun to play). Personally, I like to play a tongued short roll. With a bit of practice, it sounds really crisp. If the tune speeds up, I sometimes drop the cut so it just becomes tongue-strike. Still seems to achieve the crisp triplet effect, even though it’s not actually a triplet anymore.

↳ Posted by joshthewhistler on October 26th, 2023.

Re: Crossing The Minch
